article.articleHeadline: รัฐบาลสั่งเฝ้าระวังเข้ม ไวรัสฮันตา ย้ำไทยยังเสี่ยงต่ำ-ไม่พบระบาด - The Bangkok Insight
article.articleHeadlineTranslated: Government orders tighter surveillance for Hantavirus; Thailand remains at low risk—no outbreak detected.
article.articleSummary: Thailand tightens Hantavirus surveillance as no outbreak is detected and country remains at low risk as of May 11, 2026. The government, via the Ministry of Public Health, monitors Hantavirus after WHO reported cases linked to a cruise ship in the South Atlantic. No local cases are reported. Measures include intensified screening at international borders and strengthened domestic surveillance, with airlines, ports, and health facilities to screen travelers with rodent exposure. Hantavirus is carried by rodents; infection typically results from inhalation of dust contaminated with rodent urine or feces, while human-to-human transmission is rare and limited to certain strains. Symptoms resemble influenza, with possible respiratory involvement; there is no specific antiviral or vaccine; treatment is supportive. Officials consider designating Hantavirus as a dangerous infectious disease under the 2015 Communicable Diseases Act and will conduct risk assessments. Public urged to avoid rodent habitats and follow cleaning and disinfection guidance.

article.articleHeadline: Setengah Abad Aceh "Digigit" Anjing Gila - Serambinews.com
article.articleHeadlineTranslated: Half a Century in Aceh 'Bitten' by Rabid Dogs
article.articleSummary: As Aceh marks more than five decades since rabies was first reported in 1970, the province continues to battle the oldest and deadliest zoonotic disease. Rabies virus, from family Rhabdoviridae and genus Lyssavirus, is transmitted by rabies‑transmitting animals (RTAs) including dogs, and also by cats, monkeys, civets, bats, and foxes. Humans typically acquire infection by inhaling dust contaminated with rodent urine, feces, or saliva; direct contact and, rarely, rodent bites can occur. Person-to-person transmission is uncommon, except for the Andes strain in South America. Clinically, two syndromes exist: Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome (HFRS) common in Asia/Europe, and Hantavirus Pulmonary Syndrome (HPS) in the Americas; the Andes strain carries a 30–40% fatality rate. In Thailand, hantavirus and antibodies have been detected in rodents and in some humans, especially those exposed to rodents or agricultural work; however, prevalence is very low and multiple local rodent species carry distinct strains. Symptoms include fever, myalgia, headache, nausea/vomiting; severe disease can cause kidney failure, bleeding, pulmonary edema, and respiratory failure.

article.articleSummary: A 6-year-old from Lai Châu Province in Vietnam developed severe chickenpox with pneumococcal bacteremia, leading to rapid respiratory failure and hemorrhagic complications. He was admitted to the National Institute of Infectious and Tropical Diseases Hospital in Hanoi. Blood cultures confirmed Streptococcus pneumoniae sepsis on a background of varicella; procalcitonin was markedly elevated (>100). Despite two days of local treatment, the child’s condition worsened, requiring noninvasive then invasive mechanical ventilation. He exhibited bleeding in vesicles, epistaxis, gastrointestinal bleeding, and severe coagulopathy. After two days of high‑dose antivirals and antibiotics, bleeding and some inflammatory indices improved, but fever persisted and the illness remained severe; by day four, inflammatory markers rose again, indicating ongoing complexity. The case underscores that varicella can be associated with life‑threatening bacterial superinfection; early evaluation, wound care, and timely antiviral therapy are essential. Varicella vaccination at 12 months can reduce risk.

article.articleSummary: Hantavirus infection is a rare zoonosis transmitted mainly by inhalation of aerosolized rodent urine, saliva or droppings. Infections arise in enclosed, poorly ventilated spaces and can be triggered by dry sweeping or vacuuming. Incubation is 1–8 weeks (usually 2–3). Early symptoms mimic flu, but some patients abruptly deteriorate into hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome with severe lung and heart involvement; breathing problems often escalate within hours. Severe cases (Sin Nombre and Andes viruses) may require oxygen or ventilation; kidney involvement occurs in European and Asian variants, with reduced urine output, swelling and abnormal renal tests; dialysis may be required in advanced disease. No specific cure exists; management is supportive. Andes virus can transmit person-to-person in rare close-contact scenarios. High-risk settings include storage rooms, abandoned buildings, farm sheds and cabins. As of 11 May 2026, two Indian crew members from virus-hit MV Hondius were safe and asymptomatic; prevention emphasizes hygiene.

article.articleSummary: A Vietnamese pediatric case highlights severe chickenpox (varicella) with fatal-seeming complications. Avoid letting rats enter homes, particularly around gardens or rodent nests; maintain a healthy lifestyle to support immunity.

Avian influenza viruses, notably H5N1, have around 70% fatality but require direct contact with infected birds; most human cases occur in Asia. article.articleHeadline: What is Valley Fever? Indian techie in US dies after rare fungal infection turns fatal, leaves behind young family- Moneycontrol.com
article.articleSummary: Chiranjeevi Kolla, a 37-year-old Indian tech professional in California, died May 5, 2026 after nearly a month in ICU battling Valley fever. The fungal infection is caused by Coccidioides spores in dry soil of the southwestern United States, including California, with spores becoming airborne via wind, farming, construction or dust storms; regions also include parts of Mexico and Central/South America. article.articleSummary: Andes hantavirus, reportedly human-transmissible, highlights how climate change and ecosystem disruption raise zoonotic risk. Warmer winters and springs, more rainfall, and extreme heat boost rodent populations—deer mice in North America and bank voles in Europe—increasing contact with humans and hantavirus exposure. In New Mexico, post-rain vegetation correlates with deer mouse surges and hantavirus outbreaks; in the United States, hantavirus spikes have been linked to El Niño, which is expected to intensify. In Belgium, hot summers and autumns raise beech seed production, fueling bank vole growth and hantavirus risk; overall, warming climate may raise HPS incidence in coming decades. A July last year Science Advances study mapped global risk: 9.3% of land at high or very high risk; 3% very high; Latin America and Oceania most affected (Latin America 27.1%). WHO priority pathogens list is cited, with Disease X possibly representing Andes hantavirus.

article.articleHeadline: L'Hantavirus stroncò Gene Hackman e la moglie un anno fa: cos'è, cure, rischi
article.articleHeadlineTranslated: The Hantavirus felled Gene Hackman and his wife a year ago: what it is, treatments, risks.
article.articleSummary: Hantavirus comprises a group of single-stranded, negative-sense RNA viruses in the Hantaviridae family, mainly transmitted by rodents via urine, feces, and saliva. It can cause two diseases: hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HCPS). HCPS is more severe, with about 50% mortality, and occurs in the United States, Canada, and several South American countries, including Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil, Chile, Paraguay, Panama, and Uruguay. A winter 2025 case drew global attention: Betsy Arakawa died February 11, 2025 in Santa Fe, New Mexico from HCPS; her husband Gene Hackman died a few days later from heart failure linked to Alzheimer's. No globally approved antivirals or vaccines exist; treatment is supportive. Early ribavirin may help in HFRS; fluids, electrolytes, platelet transfusions, and respiratory support as needed (ventilation, hemofiltration, membrane oxygenation). WHO deems global risk low, with no travel/trade restrictions; stresses early diagnosis and exposure reduction; tourism poses minimal risk.

article.articleSummary: Hantavirus screening debate in India follows reports of a hantavirus affected cruise ship off Tenerife in Spain's Canary Islands. As travellers return home, authorities consider airport checks, but experts warn that rapid identification is hard in ordinary Indian hospitals; only specialised centers with sequencing can confirm the virus. Early hantavirus symptoms resemble flu, raising the risk that initial cases are missed unless an outbreak is known. Some hantavirus strains can spread via droplets, so airport screening could be useful in uncertain situations, and suspected cases should be quarantined pending diagnosis. Nevertheless, a blanket national screening program is not warranted, since hantavirus is largely zoonotic and imported cases have limited domestic transmission potential. Thermal screening is inadequate due to a long incubation period; targeted testing, symptom checks, and robust contact tracing are preferred for now, with overall India risk considered low.

article.articleSummary: Zoonotic hantavirus from rodents is spreading in Latin America, while Indonesia experiences sporadic cases, BRIN researcher Ristiyanto explains using Pavlovsky’s natural nidality concept (1964). A natural nidus is an ecological system where the virus, rodent reservoir, environment, climate, vegetation, and human activity interact stably. In Chile and Argentina, hantavirus strains, especially Andes virus, have a strong nidus; wild rodents surge with El Niño-driven rainfall and vegetation growth, boosting human–rodent contact in farming, livestock, tourism, and rural homes near forests. Andes virus can show limited human-to-human transmission, enabling clusters after spillover. In Indonesia, rodent biodiversity and interspecies competition create a dilution effect, limiting large outbreaks; urban rats (Rattus norvegicus, R. tanezumi) can carry hantavirus but transmission remains largely sporadic. Transmission is via inhalation of aerosolized rodent urine, saliva, or droppings; mitigation includes rodent control, sanitation, waste management, surveillance, laboratory capacity, climate-based early warning, and public education on dampening dried droppings with disinfectant.

article.articleHeadline: Хантавірус: що це за інфекція як передається і чи варто боятися
article.articleHeadlineTranslated: Hantavirus: What kind of infection is it, how is it transmitted, and should you be afraid?
article.articleSummary: Hantavirus infections are zoonotic diseases carried by rodents, primarily mice, voles and rats; transmission to people occurs via inhalation of dust containing urine, saliva, or feces, or through contact with contaminated materials or food. Human-to-human transmission is not expected. Globally, hantavirus infections requiring hospitalization number about 150,000–200,000 annually, with the majority in China. In Europe and Asia, the predominant illness is hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS); in North and South America, hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) is more common. Ukraine reports dozens of cases each year. Early symptoms resemble a flu-like illness—fever, headache, nausea, back pain, and urinary symptoms—progressing in severe cases to kidney failure (HFRS) or acute respiratory distress from pulmonary edema (HPS). Prevention emphasizes avoiding rodent contact, damp cleaning rather than sweeping, sealing food, keeping sleeping outdoors at bay, and regular disinfection. Peak risk occurs in late spring to autumn.

article.articleSummary: Hantavirus is a natural virus circulating in rodents, not something artificially created. In Pfizer FOIA documents, "Hantavirus pulmonary infection" appears on an Adverse Events of Special Interest list, but AESI is a monitoring signal, not evidence of causation. The WHO Polaris II pandemic exercise (April 22–23, 26 states, 600 doctors) is described as standard preparedness, not a real-world plan. Conclusion: the post is partially false.

article.articleHeadline: Como cientistas 'caçam' vírus pelo mundo para antecipar pandemias
article.articleHeadlineTranslated: How scientists 'hunt' viruses around the world to anticipate pandemics.
article.articleSummary: Researchers from Universidade Estadual de Campinas (Unicamp) study viral diversity along Brazil's BR-319, linking Manaus, Amazonas, to Porto Velho, Rondônia, using metagenomics to sequence all genetic material in environmental and animal samples. The Amazon houses one of the world's richest viral communities, with spillover risk rising as deforestation disrupts ecological barriers and increases contact between humans and wildlife. The program targets known viruses such as Oropouche (OROV), Mayaro (MAYV), dengue, and chikungunya, and also seeks novel agents in rodents (hantavirus, arenavirus) and vectors. Oropouche fever, transmitted by the maruim mosquito, has spread from southern Amazonas and northern Rondônia to Manaus and Humaitá, with exported cases reported in Europe and the United States. The metagenomic approach enables proactive surveillance, though no new urban outbreaks have been confirmed; social conditions and water quality influence field success.

article.articleHeadline: Norovirus Outbreak Explained: Common Symptoms, How It Spreads and Prevention Tips
article.articleSummary: Norovirus outbreaks rising globally in 2026 affect cruise ships and crowded spaces. In the United States and Caribbean, outbreaks on ships such as the Caribbean Princess and Rotterdam have sickened more than 100 passengers and crew in May 2026. Norovirus causes sudden vomiting, watery diarrhea, stomach cramps, nausea, fever, body aches and headache, with symptoms typically appearing 12-48 hours after exposure and dehydration as the main risk. Most people recover in 1-3 days; severe dehydration risk exists for children, older adults, and those with medical conditions. Transmission occurs via contaminated food and water, contact with infected surfaces, or close contact; sharing utensils and washrooms. Hand sanitizers are less effective; soap and water for at least 20 seconds plus bleach-based surface disinfection are recommended. No approved vaccine or medicine; prevention hinges on hygiene, food safety, and travel precautions. India remains at risk as outbreaks spread and travelers may import cases.

The work highlights the rich biodiversity of Brazil’s Atlantic Forest as a promising source for antiviral drug development.

article.articleHeadline: Hantavirus myths busted: What people are getting wrong about the virus
article.articleSummary: Hantavirus is a family of about 38 rodent-borne viruses that cause two human diseases: Hantavirus Pulmonary Syndrome (HPS), which begins with flu-like symptoms and can progress to breathing failure, and Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome (HFRS), which can cause fever, shock and kidney injury. Andes virus, circulating in Argentina and Chile and carried by the long-tailed colilargo mouse, has shown limited human-to-human transmission; this may explain some spread among MV Hondius passengers. Most infections occur after inhaling aerosolized rodent urine, droppings or saliva; bites are uncommon. HFRS is more common in Asia and Europe with 6–15% fatality by strain. There is no universal hantavirus vaccine; China and South Korea use vaccines against some Asian strains. In India, antibodies have been detected in Kerala, Tamil Nadu, and Vellore; Thottapalayam virus was identified in 1964. Prevention focuses on rodent control and avoiding exposure to rodent waste.

article.articleHeadline: Sốt cao mùa hè, cảnh giác viêm não Nhật Bản
article.articleHeadlineTranslated: High fever in summer, beware Japanese encephalitis.
article.articleSummary: As of May 7, 2026, Thanh Hoa Province, Vietnam, reported three Japanese encephalitis cases, including a fatality: a 14-year-old girl in Dong Son ward. The illness begins with high fever, headache, and vomiting and can be mistaken for common infection in children. The fatal case had not been vaccinated. Health authorities urge intensified surveillance, catch-up vaccination, and reaching 95% coverage. The virus is transmitted to humans by Culex mosquitoes; natural reservoirs include pigs and wild birds. Incubation is about 5–14 days. Early symptoms are non-specific; progression to encephalitis includes neck stiffness, severe headache, drowsiness, coma, or seizures. There is no specific treatment; care is supportive. Prevention relies on vaccination and avoiding bites. Vietnam offers Jevax, Imojev, and Jeev vaccines with age-specific schedules; children who had Jevax may be advised to switch to Imojev. Parents should bring vaccination records.

article.articleHeadline: Indonesia Prepares 21 Hospitals Amid MV Hondius Hantavirus Alert
article.articleSummary: Indonesia’s Health Ministry is mobilizing 21 sentinel hospitals across 20 provinces to bolster surveillance for hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS)–type hantavirus linked to the MV Hondius cruise ship cluster, with 198 referral hospitals designated to support responses. Sentinel sites will screen for jaundice to avoid misdiagnosis with liver disease or leptospirosis; PCR remains essential to identify hantavirus strains. The hantavirus detected in Indonesia is the HFRS Seoul virus, distinct from the MV Hondius outbreak’s HPS linked to Andes virus. The heightened surveillance followed a UK IHR NFP notification on May 7, 2026 about a Jakarta-based foreign national (initials KE) who had close contact with a confirmed hantavirus patient aboard MV Hondius. KE, who traveled with a deceased 69-year-old passenger, disembarked in Saint Helena on Apr 24 and later went to Johannesburg and Zimbabwe. PCR tests on five specimens were negative; KE remains under monitoring and quarantine at Sulianti Saroso Infectious Diseases Hospital.

article.articleHeadlineTranslated: Hantavirus outbreak: doctors warn that it's better to stay home and watch TV every day than go outside to do six things.
article.articleSummary: As of May 11, 2026, China is reporting ongoing Hantavirus infections across multiple locales. Hantavirus, carried by mice, causes Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome (HFRS); it is not human-to-human but can be severe via inhalation of contaminated dust, skin contact with rodent urine, or contaminated food. A representative case involved a man in his 30s with high fever and fatigue progressing to oliguria and rising serum creatinine; his balcony showed active mice amidst clutter. In severe HFRS, acute kidney failure, shock, and multi-organ dysfunction may occur. Lab findings include thrombocytopenia and urinary casts; timely diagnosis depends on exposure within two weeks. A domestically produced bivalent inactivated HFRS vaccine exists for high-risk groups, requiring three doses over about six months; not for the general public. Six preventive measures: wet-clean dusty storage, avoid barehanded handling of waste, avoid sleeping on the ground when camping, do not eat wild game, address mouse signs, and recognize urban risk.

article.articleHeadline: Sindan reforça alerta sobre brucelose durante o mês da saúde animal e destaca a vacinação obrigatória no Brasil
article.articleHeadlineTranslated: Sindan reiterates warning about brucellosis during Animal Health Month and highlights mandatory vaccination in Brazil.
article.articleSummary: During Brazil's Animal Health Month, a national vaccination campaign targets brucellosis, a zoonotic bacterial disease caused by Brucella. The campaign emphasizes mandatory vaccination of female cattle and buffalo calves aged 3–8 months, with many states requiring completion by May 31. Brucellosis, also known as Mediterranean fever, harms herds through abortions, infertility, and reduced productivity, risking economic losses and food-safety implications for Brazil, a major exporter of beef, pork, and poultry. Human infection occurs mainly via direct contact with infected animals or consumption of contaminated, especially unpasteurized, dairy products. Global data cite over 200 known zoonoses (WHO) and that about 60% of diseases are zoonotic (HealthforAnimals). Beyond vaccination, experts stress good herd management, sanitary controls, and continuous veterinary oversight, with integrated action among producers, veterinarians, and defense agencies to reduce transmission and support sanitary standards.

article.articleHeadline: How big of a deal is hantavirus?
article.articleSummary: Three passengers died from hantavirus on the cruise MV Hondius, attributed to the Andes variant that causes hantavirus pulmonary syndrome and can spread between humans. About 150 passengers disembarked over the weekend; 32 disembarked at St. Helena and flew home on April 24 before the outbreak was detected. In the United States, 17 American passengers are being processed in Nebraska, with quarantine likely; one has tested mildly positive for hantavirus and another has developed symptoms. The variant’s estimated case-fatality rate is around 38%. Indications of asymptomatic spread and a long incubation period raise containment challenges. Of those leaving the ship, destinations include the Philippines, United Kingdom, United States, Netherlands, Spain, Germany, Canada, France and others, underscoring international exposure and the need for self-isolation for several weeks. Uncertainty remains about how close contact drives transmission and the adequacy of containment measures.

article.articleHeadline: Indonesia, Vietnam, Cambodia introduce airport screening for hantavirus; India deploys 'viral shield'
article.articleSummary: Hantavirus outbreak on a Dutch cruise ship has prompted intensified border controls across Asia. Indonesia has instituted airport screening at Soekarno-Hatta International Airport in Jakarta with thermal scanning, visual observation, health declarations, and enhanced checks for flights from countries with reported cases; ambulances with decontamination systems are available to transport suspected patients, and travel history and contacts are assessed; the observation window can extend 40 days or more. Vietnam’s Hanoi CDC will monitor arrivals and transiting passengers at Noi Bai International Airport to detect suspected cases and isolate if needed. Cambodia has implemented preventive and screening measures at Techo International Airport. Thailand tightened border screening. India’s ICMR has mobilised 165 laboratories in a network, termed a viral shield, to prevent entry of the virus; the two Indians aboard the MV Hondius are in quarantine in the Netherlands, asymptomatic.

article.articleSummary: Michael Levitt, 2013 Nobel Prize in Chemistry laureate, spoke at the Sixth Asia Medical Health Summit about recent Hantavirus reports, urging calm and warning that panic can cause more harm than the virus; transmissibility does not imply high mortality, citing COVID-19 Omicron as an example where deaths remained limited despite rapid spread. China presents opportunities due to its large population, with screening gaps and high mobile‑health adoption offering pathways to improve health management across the region.

article.articleHeadline: Hantavirus : un virus "connu" à la contagiosité "plus faible" que le Covid-19, rassure le professeur Bruno Mégarbane - ICI
article.articleHeadlineTranslated: Hantavirus: a 'known' virus with 'lower' contagiousness than COVID-19, reassures Professor Bruno Mégarbane - ICI.
article.articleSummary: Hantavirus outbreak aboard the cruise ship MV Hondius raises comparisons with early COVID-19, but Prof. Bruno Mégarbane of Hôpital Lariboisière in Paris cautions against mirroring the pandemic trajectory. The virus, known since 1976 and previously confined to South America, appears less contagious, requiring close contact, such as kissing or sharing meals in enclosed spaces, for transmission. Transmission chains on the Hondius are reportedly identifiable as the outbreak unfolds, unlike the protracted, global spread seen with COVID-19 after it emerged in China. Lethality is high for hantavirus, with about 40-50% case fatality due to pulmonary and cardiac involvement, including acute respiratory and heart failure and possible sudden cardiac arrest. Rapid deaths limit onward transmission, whereas COVID-19 could infect thousands before fatalities accumulated. The report stresses caution without overestimating the threat, underlining containment and surveillance on ships.

article.articleHeadline: Cosa sappiamo sull'Hantavirus, malattia endemica nel Sudamerica
article.articleHeadlineTranslated: What do we know about Hantavirus, an endemic disease in South America.
article.articleSummary: Hantaviruses cause hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) and hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS). Transmission is mainly zoonotic via inhalation of rodent excreta or direct contact; human-to-human spread is rare and limited to close contact with symptomatic cases. In Europe, Puumala and Dobrava viruses cause nephropathic syndromes through inhalation of rodent secretions, with no documented human-to-human transmission. In the Americas, as of week 47 of 2025, eight countries—Argentina, Brazil, Bolivia, Chile, United States, Panama, Paraguay, and Uruguay—reported confirmed HPS cases totaling 229 with 59 deaths (about 25.7% mortality). An Argentina-origin outbreak linked to the cruise ship Hondius caused at least three deaths and around ten positive passengers (not all symptomatic), with repatriation and quarantine planned on arrival in the Canary Islands. HPS symptoms resemble influenza: fever, myalgia, chills, headache, nausea, vomiting, sometimes abdominal pain; progression can lead to hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome; no specific therapy.

article.articleHeadline: 'É inútil ceder ao pânico', diz epidemiologista que acompanhou surto de hantavírus na Argentina
article.articleHeadlineTranslated: "It's no use giving in to panic," says the epidemiologist who tracked the hantavirus outbreak in Argentina.
article.articleSummary: Argentina’s Andes South hantavirus outbreak on the cruise MV Hondius underscores that human-to-human transmission remains exceptional for hantaviruses. The Andes virus, the only hantavirus with documented human transmission, is carried by the Andean-Patagonian cordillera rodents (Oligoryzomys longicaudatus). In 1995 Bariloche region in Río Negro/Patagonia experienced the first major human-to-human outbreak, prompting biosafety reforms after losses to tourism and local economies; a later Chubut outbreak of 34 people highlighted consequences of inadequate isolation. Current discussions by epidemiologist Edmundo Larrieu emphasize that panic is irrational; while lethal, transmission among people can be prevented with strict biosafety: case isolation, protective masks, and tracking close contacts. The cordillera spans Neuquén, Río Negro, Chubut, Santa Cruz, and Tierra del Fuego, with sporadic cases annually; on the MV Hondius, a possible initial rodent exposure (pre- or onboard) sparked transmission, mitigated by rapid contact tracing and isolation. Incubation about 15–20 days; eradication is unlikely.

article.articleSummary: COVID-19 is caused by SARS-CoV-2, detected in Wuhan, China, in late 2019; WHO declared a pandemic on 11 March 2020, with millions of deaths and major economic impact. Hantavirus, named after the Hantaan River, is worldwide—common in Asia and Europe—with transmission to humans mainly from infected wild rodents via inhalation of dust contaminated with their excreta. The Andes hantavirus is the only strain with documented human-to-human transmission; incubation is 1–6 weeks (longer than COVID-19’s ~7–10 days). Close proximity exposure is required for Andes transmission, especially before symptoms appear. Americas hantaviruses can cause respiratory and cardiac distress and hemorrhagic fever; COVID-19 is a respiratory illness with fever, cough, dyspnea, headache, myalgia, fatigue, diarrhea, and anosmia. No hantavirus-specific treatment or vaccine exists; rapid care improves prognosis, possibly requiring ventilation or dialysis. For COVID-19, vaccines (including mRNA) and antivirals exist, with efficacy and safety documented in billions of doses.

article.articleHeadline: Troubled waters: Jakarta battles deadly, invasive suckerfish - kuwaitTimes
article.articleSummary: Jakarta battles an invasive sapu-sapu (suckermouth catfish/pleco) introduced from South America decades ago to keep aquarium algae in check. Flourishing in Java’s polluted rivers, it outcompetes native fish, preys on eggs, and weakens riverbanks by digging nests. The species can reach about 0.5 m, and females lay thousands of eggs yearly. In Greater Jakarta, where 42 million people rely on stressed water systems, more than half of rivers are heavily polluted and only about 7.4% of municipal wastewater is safely treated. Critics urge cleanup of polluted waste rather than mass slaughter. As of May 2026.

article.articleHeadline: Ultraschallwellen als potenzielle Waffe gegen Viren
article.articleHeadlineTranslated: Ultrasound waves as a potential weapon against viruses
article.articleSummary: São Paulo/London — Researchers at the University of São Paulo report a method using ultrasound waves to destroy viruses, including SARS-CoV-2 and Influenza A. In laboratory studies, ultrasound frequencies between 3 and 20 MHz induced physical changes in viral envelopes, leading to disruption while leaving surrounding cells unharmed, indicating selective action. The approach relies on acoustic resonance: matching the sound-wave frequency to the virus shell’s natural vibration, amplifying damage to the viral envelope. Because it targets physical structures, the method could remain effective against mutated viruses. The researchers also speculate applicability to Dengue, Zika, and Chikungunya. article.articleSummary: Hantavirus cases on a ship traveling from Argentina to Cabo Verde prompt the WHO to say pandemic risk is extremely low. The vessel docked in Tenerife, Canary Islands (Spain), disembarking 94 passengers from 19 nationalities, with 52 more to be released the next day. Brazil’s Health Ministry says the South American–linked outbreak does not threaten Brazil, and there is no human transmission domestically. Minas Gerais confirmed Brazil’s first hantavirus death, an isolated February case.

article.articleHeadline: Infecția cu hantavirus "nu este un nou COVID-19", potrivit experților în medicină - ARADON
article.articleHeadlineTranslated: Hantavirus infection "is not a new COVID-19," according to medical experts - ARADON
article.articleSummary: Hantavirus infection is not a new COVID-19, WHO experts told AFP. Although the MV Hondius cruise incident, bound for Netherlands, revived pandemic memories, hantavirus and COVID-19 differ. COVID-19 began in 2019 in Wuhan, China, and was declared a pandemic on 11 March 2020. Hantavirus, named after the Hantan River, is found worldwide, with Asia and Europe as endemic regions. It is mainly transmitted to humans by wild rodents via saliva, urine and droppings; inhalation of contaminated dust is the main route. The Anzi strain detected on the Hondius can spread between humans only under close proximity and specific vulnerabilities; general transmission is limited. American hantaviruses can cause respiratory and cardiac failure and hemorrhagic fever; COVID-19 is a respiratory illness with varied symptoms. There is no specific hantavirus treatment or vaccine; rapid care improves prognosis, requiring ventilation or dialysis. COVID-19 vaccines (mRNA) and antivirals exist. Argentina reported 11 deaths in 2018–2019.

article.articleHeadlineTranslated: Hantavirus in South America: rising alert, high case-fatality among reported cases in 2025 - The Voice of Italy

In 2025, through week 47, eight Americas countries logged 229 confirmed hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) cases and 59 deaths, a regional case-fatality rate of 25.7%. Prevention focuses on avoiding rodent exposure and contaminated environments, with sustained surveillance and international cooperation needed.

article.articleHeadline: Лопаются как попкорн. В Бразилии нашли способ уничтожать COVID-19 и грипп ультразвуком
article.articleHeadlineTranslated: They burst like popcorn. In Brazil, a method to destroy COVID-19 and influenza with ultrasound has been found.
article.articleSummary: As of May 11, 2026, researchers at the University of São Paulo in Brazil demonstrated in vitro destruction of influenza A and SARS-CoV-2 using ultrasound. Viruses exposed to 3–20 MHz experienced acoustic resonance that disrupts the viral envelope, rendering them non-infectious while host cells remained unharmed; temperature and pH stayed constant, excluding chemical or thermal damage. The effect, described as viral particles “exploding” under resonance, exploits the sphere-shaped envelope’s energy absorption. Because the approach targets the physical shell, viral genetic changes should not undermine efficacy. Published in Scientific Reports, the study suggests a mutation-robust, environmentally friendly alternative to chemical antivirals, with no waste and no resistance risk. Ongoing work includes Dengue, Zika, and Chikungunya viruses; clinical application remains distant.

article.articleHeadline: CARPHA Says Caribbean Risk Remains Low After Hantavirus Outbreak
article.articleSummary: Eight hantavirus cases (confirmed and suspected) and three deaths are reported in an outbreak linked to the Dutch-registered cruise MV Hondius, with Caribbean risk considered low as of May 11, 2026. Passengers and crew from 28 countries—including the United States, United Kingdom, Philippines, and the Netherlands—have been affected; several individuals have been evacuated or repatriated and international contact tracing is underway. The ship departed Argentina on April 1 and was reported to the WHO on May 2 after a cluster of respiratory illness. The outbreak is caused by the Andes strain of hantavirus, the only known strain capable of person-to-person spread, though transmission is very rare and requires close, prolonged contact. article.articleHeadlineTranslated: What is hantavirus and why it paralyzes the world with horror - World
article.articleSummary: Three deaths on the cruise ship Hondius in Tenerife brought hantavirus into sharp focus. Named from the Han River region in Korea, hantaviruses are carried by rodents and shed in urine, feces, and saliva. Humans typically become infected by inhaling dust contaminated with dried excreta; direct bites or skin wounds can also spread the virus. Old World strains are widespread across Europe and Asia (Balkans, Russia, China, Nordic countries); Sin Nombre circulates in the Americas (USA, Canada, Argentina, Chile). Two clinical pictures: hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) causing fever, bleeding, and kidney failure; mortality 1-15%; and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) with rapid lung edema and about 40% mortality. Human-to-human transmission is rare; no vaccine or specific antiviral—supportive care only. Bulgaria notes risk in mountainous/forested areas around Smolyan, Devin, Velingrad, Blagoevgrad region; summer/fall peaks; diagnostics rely on IgM/IgG antibodies, with IgM indicating acute infection.
